meta.regime: A weekend re-verification pass broke three of this report's own numbers, and all three broke the same way: positions were being carried on figures that were either stale or never checked against a second source. Sterling goes to 0 because the November hike it was scored on is priced at 81% by the rates market and expected by roughly one in eight economists polled by Reuters, which is the widest market-versus-forecaster gap on this board and the opposite of a consensus. The French budget vote that justified holding the euro short into a binary event is not on Tuesday - the Assembly debates from October 13 to 19 and votes on the revenue half on October 20 - while euro-area bank equity, which yesterday's report called stabilised, is down about 8% over two weeks and entered a technical correction on Thursday. And the BoJ October meeting this report called the most under-priced lean on the board is priced near 25% in futures, not the 6% carried yesterday, so the gap being traded does not exist.
meta.nextBigEvent: US September CPI on Wednesday October 14 at 12:30 UTC, where headline is seen accelerating to 3.6-3.7% from 3.4% on roughly 5% energy and 9% gasoline gains while core is forecast at 0.2% m/m and the Cleveland Fed nowcast sits at 0.20%; the French Assembly's first solemn vote, on the budget's revenue half, follows on October 20 rather than this Tuesday.

dailyRead: This is a Sunday report, so no price has moved since Friday's close and every market level below is the October 9 close re-verified on TradingEconomics this morning. What a weekend buys is the one thing a daily cycle rarely has time for, which is checking the report's own numbers against a second source rather than carrying them forward. Three of them did not survive that check, and because this report has been scoring currencies off those numbers, the corrections are the content today rather than a footnote to it. First and most consequential, sterling. Yesterday GBP was cut from +2 to +1 on the argument that the record gilt yield is a fiscal premium rather than a policy one, and that argument stands and is if anything better documented today: the 30-year went through 6% around October 1 for the first time since early 1998, the October 28 Budget arrives with Chancellor Healey's headroom cut to roughly 13.8bn pounds from 26bn on one estimate and about 12bn from 23.6bn on another, and the Bank of England has paused its gilt sales and set aside 120bn pounds of its longest-dated stock to back banknotes, which is an institution managing a long end rather than tightening into it. But yesterday's report also wrote that the hawkish leg was intact and arguably stronger than it was, and that is the part that fails. The November 5 hike is priced at 81% by the rates market on LSEG data, and only around one in eight economists polled by Reuters expects it. That is not a hawkish consensus with a sceptical fringe, it is a rates market and a forecasting community that disagree almost completely, and the standing rule here is to prefer polls and market pricing over the report's own prior framing. A currency cannot be scored a point above neutral when the single thing holding it there is a hike that only one of its two constituencies believes in. Two smaller corrections come with it: TradingEconomics now carries the ten-year gilt at 5.4226%, not the 5.4457% used yesterday, which makes it plus 5bp on the week rather than plus 7bp and 18.56bp over the Treasury rather than 20.87bp, and August GDP out Thursday is forecast at minus 0.1% m/m on the ForexFactory calendar after plus 0.4%, not the minus 0.3% to minus 0.4% this report wrote. The gilt is still the highest major yield in the world and still the only one up on the week. Sterling still did not move, closing 1.32327 and minus 0.07% on the week. GBP goes to 0, the forward goes to balanced, and seven BoE speeches between Monday and Saturday - Bailey four times, including a red folder at 02:00 UTC on Friday - are where the 81% either gets defended or starts converging on the economists. Second, the euro, where yesterday's upgrade from -2 to -1 was right in level and wrong in both stated reasons. The upgrade rested on two channels having stopped working. One of them genuinely did, and by more than was claimed: OAT-Bund is 138.13bp on TradingEconomics against the Bund at 3.4860% and the OAT at 4.8673%, and the narrowing is not the 141 to 139 to 138 drift described yesterday but a move down from above 150bp on October 2 and reporting of roughly 159bp the Friday before that, the widest since November 2011, with the French ten-year having been above 5% and at 4.96% at its peak, the highest since 2002. That is a real and large improvement in the sovereign channel. The other channel did not stop. Bloomberg published on October 10 - after yesterday's report was written - that European bank stocks have fallen about 8% over two weeks to their lowest since June and entered a technical correction on Thursday, with Societe Generale, Credit Agricole and Deutsche Bank all more than 15% below recent highs, under the headline that the swoon is a sign of caution rather than panic. Friday's plus 0.51% in the bank index was one session inside that drawdown, and this report read it as a turn. The third correction is a calendar one and it is the most tradeable thing in this report. Yesterday's nextBigEvent was the French National Assembly opening its 2027 budget debate on Tuesday October 13, described as a binary event three sessions out. The Assembly's published timetable is that the first part is debated in open session from Tuesday October 13 to Monday October 19, with the solemn vote on the revenue half on Tuesday October 20, the social security bill voted October 27, and the whole text on November 17. There is no vote on Tuesday and therefore no censure trigger on Tuesday. The politics are also less binary than yesterday's wording: La France Insoumise's Panot has said the group will censure whatever happens, but LFI and the left reached 260 of the 289 votes needed in February, and the Rassemblement National, which holds the decisive bloc, has had Le Pen say she prefers an imperfect budget that is operational before the elections to a loi speciale that cannot be amended afterwards. Lecornu's own public position has moved to no 49.3, no ordinances and a vote in the end, qualified by parliamentary obstruction, against earlier reporting that he kept ordinances open - the sources genuinely conflict and that is worth stating rather than resolving. Net of all of it the euro stays at -1: it is not upgraded to 0 because the bank channel is still firing, and not returned to -2 because the sovereign channel has improved materially and the swing voter has signalled passage. EUR/USD closed 1.11959, minus 0.53% on the week and minus 3.58% on the month, still the worst major. Third, the yen, where the correction removes a trade rather than changing a score. This report has carried the BoJ October 30 meeting as priced at 6% against a former executive director's 20-30%, and called that the most under-priced lean on the board. Overnight-rate futures price the October 30 hike at about 25-26%, and Kazuo Momma's 20-30% sits inside that, not above it. The market and the former insider agree, so there is no gap to trade. What remains is real but smaller: Ueda said on October 6 that the Bank intends to continue raising the policy rate and adjusting the degree of accommodation in response to developments in activity, prices and financial conditions, which Bloomberg read as doing little to challenge bets against a back-to-back move; TradingEconomics' own forecast row for October 30 is 1.25%, a hold; and futures price most of one hike by December and 2.02% by September 2027. The bond market is still doing the hawkish work - the ten-year JGB closed 3.0159% for minus 10bp on the week, the largest rally on any major curve, after the October 6 auction cleared at 3.101% near a three-decade high - and the Treasury-JGB gap is still 222.11bp, so carry still pays and USD/JPY closed 158.226, plus 0.23% on the week and plus 2.46% on the month. JPY stays at 0, the forward goes from hawkish to balanced, and the October 30 Outlook Report and its inflation revision is now the whole event rather than a formality attached to an under-priced meeting. Fourth, the dollar, held at +2 with its own December number restated honestly. Yesterday's report said December pricing had slipped from roughly 84% into a 65-81% range. The sources available today span wider than that in both directions: the CME term structure on October 7 carried 67.5% for a 4.00-4.25% target and 17.7% for 4.25-4.50%, which sums to roughly 85% cumulative for at least one hike, while one aggregator shows 62.3% cumulative and Kalshi sits near 65%. So the correct statement is that December is priced somewhere between about 62% and 85% depending on whose curve you read, and the dispersion is the fact, not a markdown. October 28 is a hold at 78-84% with the hike near 17-22%, down from about 51% a week earlier. The Fed's own September projections carry 4.1% for end-2026 against a 4.00% upper bound now, which is one more hike, and 3.9% for 2027. DXY closed 102.213, plus 0.28% on the week, plus 3.20% on the month and plus 3.96% year to date, and the thesis from yesterday survives its own correction: a dollar that holds through a 23-point spread in its own December probability is a dollar being paid for other people's problems rather than its own path. Wednesday's CPI is the test and the shape is the point - Barclays has energy up about 5% m/m with gasoline near 9%, Continuum about 5.5% on energy, RBC headline at plus 0.6% m/m taking the annual rate to 3.7%, against core at 0.2% m/m and a Cleveland Fed nowcast of 0.20% and 2.39%. A core at 0.3% or above revives an October meeting; 0.2% or below leaves December as the only live date and takes this score to +1. Fifth, oil, where two supply facts arrived that this report did not have. Hurricane Isaias forced operators to shut in more than 60% of Gulf of Mexico crude production capacity, and the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen to a near-record low. Those sit on top of the Hormuz picture, where 10 to 12 tankers were struck in the week to October 4 on Kpler and Reuters counts against a previous weekly high of six, transits fell to seven tankers on one day - the lowest since July 23 - and roughly 9.5 million barrels a day left the strait, about 30% below prewar on Kpler's measure. Against all of that WTI closed 91.660, plus 0.60% on the week and minus 10.56% on the month, while Brent closed 104.430 and plus 2.13% on the week after a 4% day on October 8 that peaked above 105 before Trump said the US would not strike Iran before the November 3 midterms. The Brent-over-WTI performance split is the tell: Hormuz is a Brent problem and the hurricane is a WTI problem, and the political cap is holding the second down more effectively than the first. USOIL stays RANGE, but with two unpriced bullish supply legs rather than one, and a WTI break higher is still the first thing that would force a revisit of CAD. Sixth, the two currencies where nothing needed correcting. The Australian dollar was the only G10 currency higher against the dollar on the week at 0.69833 and plus 0.38%, on the highest cash rate in the bloc at 4.60% and copper at 6.6630, plus 2.63% on the week and plus 38.87% on the year with refined-copper tariffs still unresolved, capped by iron ore at 90.68 and minus 8.11% on the month, which is the larger export. It stays +1. The franc stays at 0 with the same contradiction intact: the SNB is at 0% after a fifth hold, dropped its specific bias against rapid appreciation in September, and had Vice Chairman Martin hint at lower-for-longer on October 8, and the franc was bid anyway, with EUR/CHF at 0.92891 down a third straight week. Note the week-versus-day distinction yesterday's report blurred - USD/CHF fell 0.32% on Friday but was plus 0.04% on the week and plus 2.00% on the month, so the franc is strong against the euro, not against the dollar. Chairman Schlegel speaks Thursday and the minutes land October 22. Finally the cleanest tickets, and one of them has to be re-rated downward even though it stays the best thing here. AUD/NZD LONG still has the structure: 185bp between an RBA at 4.60% and an RBNZ at 2.75%, with the RBNZ deciding October 28, six days before the RBA, and TradingEconomics' forecast rows carrying 2.75% for October and 3.00% for December in line with the Bank's own September track. What has changed is the kicker. This report has been long on the argument that the market prices 58% for an October hike against a bank pointing to a pause, so the repricing was the trade. The current reading available today is 88% for no change, which would mean that repricing has already happened - and the 58% is not re-verifiable this morning. So AUD/NZD stays the top pick but as a carry-and-sequencing trade rather than a repricing one, and the conviction stays MED rather than being raised. Beyond it the honest list is short: EUR/AUD and EUR/CHF SHORT are the two cleanest expressions of the euro's remaining weakness, USD/CAD LONG is backed by the widest score gap on the board though the pair closed plus 0.01% on the week and refused to extend on a 74K employment miss, and NZD/USD SHORT has the weakest data set in the G10 behind it. There is no HIGH conviction anywhere today, as yesterday: the setting has paid on 0 of 5 calls over the last 24 reports, and a Sunday priced off a two-day-old close is the last place to reintroduce it. Four biases flip. GBP/JPY goes from LONG to RANGE and GBP/AUD from RANGE to SHORT, both purely on the sterling downgrade. Gold and silver go from LONG to RANGE, because real yields near 17-year highs are steering the metals more than the war is, Friday's lift was a strong 30-year Treasury auction rather than a haven bid, and holding a LONG in a metal that is minus 2.86% on the month against a central bank still expected to hike once more was the same mistake as the three corrected above - a position carried past the evidence for it.

today.read: The backward verdict is unchanged and easy - this is the weakest data set in the G10 relative to its policy rate. Q2 CPI ran 4.1% against a 1-3% target with core at 3.2%, growth slowed to plus 0.2% q/q from plus 0.9%, unemployment rose to 5.6% from 5.4%, and NZD/USD closed 0.56120, minus 0.04% on the week and minus 3.19% on the month near one-year lows, with the ten-year at 5.0703%. The forward is where the honesty is needed. For three sessions this report has been short the kiwi and long AUD/NZD on a specific mechanism: the market prices roughly 58% for an October hike, the RBNZ's own September track points to an October pause then a December move, TE's forecast rows carry 2.75% for October 28 and 3.00% for December 9 in line with the Bank, and the repricing of that 58% was the payoff. The 58% is not re-verifiable this morning. The figure that is available is 88% for no change from a probability tracker whose page metadata is stale enough that it should be treated with caution rather than relied on - but it is the only current reading, and if it is even approximately right then the market has already come into line with the Bank and the kicker is spent. The structural case survives intact: 185bp between an RBA at 4.60% and an RBNZ at 2.75%, and the RBNZ deciding six days before the RBA. So AUD/NZD stays the best thing on this board and its conviction stays MED rather than being raised, because it is now a carry-and-sequencing trade rather than a repricing one. Q3 CPI on October 21 is the only thing that can force October and an acceleration from 4.1% is what reverses this score; the Governor speaks October 15 and a general election follows November 7.

EUR.when: October 29, with the deposit rate at 2.50% and a hold the base case.
EUR.note: TE re-verified the Deposit Facility Rate at 2.50% against a main refinancing rate of 2.65% and a marginal lending rate of 2.90%. September HICP at 3.8% from 3.2% and core at 2.5% argue the direction is still up, and roughly 80% has been priced for another move by year-end, against Lane's caveat that higher borrowing costs could reduce the need to tighten. GBP.when: November 5, with a Monetary Policy Report, priced at 81% on LSEG data but expected by only about one in eight economists polled by Reuters.
GBP.note: Held at 3.75% on September 17 on a 6-3 vote, the three dissenters wanting 25bp to 4.00%. This is the field where the report's own framing has to change: yesterday it called the hawkish leg intact and arguably stronger, and an 81% market against a roughly 12% forecaster consensus is not a strengthening case, it is the widest disagreement on this board. The committee noise is real - Greene pressed for a hike on October 8, Breeden and Lombardelli back the energy argument against Dhingra - and UK gas at 199.64 GBp/thm, plus 6.14% on the week and plus 170.48% on the year, is that argument in one number. Against it: the Bank has paused gilt sales and set aside 120bn pounds of its longest-dated stock to back banknotes, the 30-year went through 6% around October 1 for the first time since early 1998, the October 28 Budget arrives with headroom cut to roughly 13.8bn pounds from 26bn on one estimate, and August GDP on October 15 is forecast at minus 0.1% m/m. Seven BoE speeches run October 12-17; September CPI on October 21 is the decider. Market pricing carries about 90bp of tightening by end-2027.

JPY.when: December is the market's date, with October 30 priced near 25-26% in overnight-rate futures rather than the 6% this report carried.
JPY.note: Hiked to 1.25% on September 18 on a 7-2 vote with Asada and Sato dissenting, the highest policy rate in 31 years. The correction matters more than the level: futures put October 30 at about 25-26% and former BoJ executive director Kazuo Momma puts consecutive hikes at 20-30%, which is inside the market rather than above it, so the under-priced gap this report has been trading does not exist. Momma also said the chance of delaying past January is extremely low. Ueda said on October 6 that the Bank intends to keep raising the policy rate and adjusting accommodation in response to activity, prices and financial conditions, which Bloomberg read as doing little to challenge bets against a back-to-back move, and TE's own forecast row for October 30 is 1.25%. Futures price most of one hike by December and 2.02% by September 2027. October 30 carries the Quarterly Outlook Report, and the inflation forecast revision is now the whole tradeable event.

AUD.note: Hiked to 4.60% on September 29 in a unanimous vote, the fourth of 2026, the highest cash rate in the G10 and the highest Australian rate since 2011, after which Bullock signalled less follow-up tightening than futures had carried. The near-term sequence is the September minutes on October 13, China September CPI on October 14, then September employment on October 15 - a red folder at 00:30 UTC, forecast at plus 20.0K after plus 39.5K with unemployment held at 4.6% - and then Q3 CPI on October 28, six days before the meeting, which is what actually decides it.

NZD.when: October 28, where the available current reading is 88% for no change - which would mean the repricing this report was positioned for has already happened.
NZD.note: Hiked to 2.75% on September 2. TE's forecast rows carry 2.75% for October 28 and 3.00% for December 9, siding with the Bank's own September track of an October pause then a December move. The honest correction is on the market leg: this report has been trading a market at 58% against that track, and 58% is not re-verifiable this morning, while the current figure available is 88% no-change from a probability tracker whose metadata is stale enough to treat with caution. If 88% is right the fade is largely done and what remains in AUD/NZD is carry and sequencing rather than a repricing kicker. Q3 CPI on October 21, one week before the decision, is the only thing that can force October; Q2 ran 4.1% against a 1-3% target with core at 3.2%, while Q2 growth slowed to plus 0.2% q/q and unemployment rose to 5.6%. The Governor speaks October 15 and a general election follows November 7.

CAD.when: October 28, with a Monetary Policy Report - confirmed on the Bank's own calendar, followed by December 9.
CAD.note: Held at 2.25% on September 2 for a seventh consecutive decision. The dovish-leaning hold stands: after the September employment report markets still carried roughly 27% odds of an October hike with nothing priced for a cut, and TD read the print as cooling hike talk rather than building a cut case. What the data did is real - employment fell 68.3K against a plus 6.1K forecast after August's minus 41.7K, unemployment rose to 6.5% and participation dropped to 64.8%, the lowest since December 1997 excluding 2020 - so Macklem's September line that firms were slowing hiring rather than cutting no longer survives contact. Macklem speaks October 14 and October 16, the Survey of Consumer Expectations lands October 19 with September CPI, and August held at 3.0% headline with core at 2.4%.

The claim being withdrawn is that this was the most under-priced lean on the board: that rested on a 6% market against former executive director Kazuo Momma's 20-30% for consecutive hikes, and futures actually price October 30 at about 25-26%, so Momma sits inside the market rather than above it and the gap is gone. The structural change is still real: Takaichi telling parliament Japan no longer needs reflationary policy built on monetary easing and fiscal expansion is a supply story, and the curve rallied 10bp on hawkish news because less fiscal expansion means less issuance. The counterweights are tactical: the 222.11bp carry still pays and no session has sustained a break of the 158.50 area since late September. October 30 is an Outlook Report, and its inflation forecast revision is now the whole tradeable event. Invalidated if that report drops the overshoot language or if core CPI, at 1.7%, keeps undershooting.

The politics have also softened at the margin that matters - LFI's Panot says the group will censure whatever happens, but LFI and the left reached 260 of the 289 needed in February, and Le Pen, whose bloc is decisive, prefers an imperfect budget operational before the elections to a loi speciale that cannot be amended afterwards. Lecornu's public line has moved to no 49.3, no ordinances and a vote in the end, qualified by parliamentary obstruction, against earlier reporting that kept ordinances open; the sources conflict and that is reported rather than resolved. On policy the Council still sounds closer to hiking than its bond market allows, with roughly 80% priced for another move by year-end against Lane's caveat on borrowing costs, and a hold expected October 29. Q3 CPI on October 21 is the only thing that can force October; the Governor speaks October 15 and the general election is November 7. catalysts.event: France: Assembly solemn vote on the whole 2027 budget
catalysts.note: The vote that closes the first reading, after the revenue half on October 20 and the social security bill on October 27. It is the last of the three scheduled points at which the government can fall on this budget, and the reason the euro's political risk is a November story as much as an October one.

catalysts.event: US: FOMC decision with projections (December 8-9)
catalysts.note: The meeting priced anywhere between about 62% and 85% depending on whose curve is read - the CME term structure on October 7 summed to roughly 85% cumulative, one aggregator showed 62.3% and Kalshi sat near 65%. It carries a new Summary of Economic Projections and dot plot, where the 2027 path gets re-set against a current median of 3.9%. Most September participants expected another increase by year-end and this is the last meeting at which that can happen.

catalysts.event: Switzerland: SNB policy assessment
catalysts.note: The next scheduled SNB decision, with the policy rate at 0% and intervention rather than negative rates as the stated tool. October 8 commentary pushed back on near-term tightening and the vice chairman hinted at lower-for-longer, so only a disorderly franc appreciation out of a euro-area sovereign event would bring this forward in practice. Chairman Schlegel speaks October 15 and the minutes land October 22.

catalysts.event: Hormuz attacks plus the Gulf of Mexico shut-in and a near-record-low SPR
catalysts.note: Two supply legs now, not one. Hurricane Isaias forced operators to shut in more than 60% of Gulf of Mexico crude production capacity and the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen to a near-record low. On top of that, 10 to 12 tankers were struck transiting Hormuz in the week to October 4 on Kpler and Reuters counts against a previous weekly high of six, transits fell to seven tankers on one day - the lowest since July 23 - and roughly 9.5 million barrels a day left the strait, about 30% below prewar on Kpler's measure. US forces have struck five IRGC-linked tankers after attempted attacks on a US warship. The price has refused to pay: WTI 91.660 and minus 10.56% on the month, Brent 104.430 and plus 2.13% on the week after a 4% day on October 8 that peaked above 105 before Trump's no-strike pledge. The Brent-over-WTI split is the tell - Hormuz is Brent's problem, the hurricane is WTI's, and the political cap binds WTI hardest.

catalysts.event: The 81% BoE hike against a one-in-eight economist consensus
catalysts.note: The new watch-item on this board and the reason GBP is scored 0. LSEG data has November 5 at 81%; only around one in eight economists polled by Reuters expects it. That is not a hawkish case with a sceptical fringe, it is two constituencies in near-total disagreement, and whichever one moves sets sterling's next point. The test runs daily through the seven-speech week to October 17 and resolves on September CPI on October 21. The related fiscal signal is the 30-year through 6% around October 1 for the first time since early 1998, with the Bank having paused gilt sales and set aside 120bn pounds of its longest-dated stock to back banknotes.

catalysts.event: Euro-area bank equity as the sovereign transmission channel
catalysts.note: The channel this report wrongly called stabilised yesterday. Bloomberg reported on October 10 that European bank stocks have fallen about 8% over two weeks to their lowest since June and entered a technical correction on Thursday, with Societe Generale, Credit Agricole and Deutsche Bank all more than 15% below recent highs, framed as caution rather than panic. Friday's plus 0.51% was one session inside that drawdown. Banks own the paper, so this is how a French political event reaches EU50, where they are the heaviest sector - and whether they lead or lag from here is the cleanest tell on whether the euro belongs at -1 or back at -2. Morgan Stanley's view is that derailing bank fundamentals would take a more prolonged period of spread widening than this.

catalysts.event: UK and European gas prices as the BoE and equity-index input
catalysts.note: UK gas at 199.64 GBp/thm is plus 2.03% on the day, plus 6.14% on the week and plus 170.48% on the year. EU gas at 80.25 EUR/MWh is plus 7.35% on the week and plus 184.98% on the year, with German gas at 79.27 plus 4.61% on the week and plus 164.21% on the year. This is the number behind Lombardelli's line that rates may need to rise if energy prices stay elevated, and it is a larger headwind for German industry than Brent at plus 2.13% on the week is a tailwind - the reason GER40 stays capped even on a relief bounce.

catalysts.event: Copper versus iron ore as the Australian terms-of-trade split
catalysts.note: Copper at 6.6630 USD/lb is plus 2.63% on the week, plus 3.03% on the month and plus 38.87% on the year, the strongest physical commodity on this board, having closed September at 6.6215 with refined-copper tariffs unresolved as a live upside risk. Iron ore at 90.68 is minus 0.73% on the week, minus 8.11% on the month and minus 15.36% on the year. Iron ore is the larger Australian export, which is the reason AUD stays at +1 rather than being promoted on the copper headline. China September CPI on October 14 is the next read on both.

geopolitics: The oil channel still splits into a physical leg and a political leg pointing opposite ways, and this week the physical leg gained a second, entirely non-political component that this report did not previously have. Hurricane Isaias forced operators in the Gulf of Mexico to shut in more than 60% of the region's crude production capacity, and the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen to a near-record low - so the United States is losing domestic supply at the same moment its buffer is thinnest. That sits on top of the Hormuz picture, which remains at wartime intensity. Between 10 and 12 tankers were struck transiting the Strait in the week to October 4 on Kpler and Reuters counts, against a previous weekly high of six; transits fell to seven tankers on one day, the lowest since July 23; and roughly 9.5 million barrels a day left the strait that week, about 30% below prewar levels on Kpler's measure. US forces have struck five IRGC-linked oil tankers after attempted Iranian attacks on a US warship, according to Central Command. Politically the opposite holds, and it is holding firmly: Trump has described productive discussions with Iran and pledged not to attack before the November 3 midterms, which took Brent off an intraday peak above 105 on October 8 after a 4% day. The price verdict is where the information is. WTI closed Friday at 91.660, up 0.19% on the day and 0.60% on the week but still minus 10.56% on the month. Brent closed 104.430, up 0.14% on the day and 2.13% on the week. That divergence is the single most useful thing in this paragraph: Brent carries the Hormuz risk and WTI carries the Gulf of Mexico outage, and the market is paying more for the first than the second even though the second is a physical barrel that is genuinely not being produced right now. The reading is that the political cap is binding WTI hardest, which is why USOIL stays RANGE rather than LONG - but it now has two unpriced bullish supply legs underneath it rather than one, and the November 3 pledge has an expiry date. The FX reads follow. First, Canada. WTI is the barrel Canada prices against, and a crude benchmark minus 10.56% on the month is why a CAD score of -2 and a labour market down 110K jobs in two months sit together coherently. But the two theses are driven by different things - the oil call is event-driven and the CAD call data-driven - and the new supply facts cut against the short at the margin, which is one reason to note that USD/CAD closed plus 0.01% on the week after absorbing a 74K employment miss. If WTI breaks this range upward, CAD is the first score this report revisits. Second, the energy inflation actually moving central banks is gas, not crude, and it got worse again: UK gas at 199.64 GBp/thm is up 6.14% on the week and 170.48% on the year, EU gas up 7.35% on the week and 184.98% on the year, German gas up 4.61% on the week and 164.21% on the year. That is the real content of Lombardelli's line that rates may need to rise if energy prices stay elevated - and it is the strongest remaining argument for the 81% priced for November 5 against a one-in-eight economist consensus, as well as the reason gas is a heavier headwind for GER40 than Brent is a tailwind. Third, the haven bid is going to the franc rather than to gold, and more precisely than this report said yesterday: EUR/CHF fell a third consecutive week to 0.92891 while USD/CHF was actually plus 0.04% on the week and plus 2.00% on the month, so the franc is winning against the euro and losing to the dollar. Gold at 4,193.87 and silver at 60.802 rose 1.47% and 2.75% on Friday, but the driver was a strong 30-year Treasury auction cooling the long end, not war, and both remain in drawdown - gold minus 2.86% on the month and minus 2.92% year to date, silver minus 14.68% year to date and roughly half its January 29 peak of 121.62. With real yields near 17-year highs steering the metals more than the conflict is, both go to RANGE today. Fourth, and the thing to carry into Monday: the event most likely to move this board is not in the Gulf, and it is not on Tuesday either. The French Assembly debates the 2027 budget in open session from October 13 to 19 and takes its first solemn vote, on the revenue half, on October 20 - a week later than this report had it - with the social security bill on October 27 and the whole text on November 17. The nearest binary event is therefore US September CPI on Wednesday, where core at 0.2% m/m is the number that decides whether the dollar stays at +2.
